Molecular mechanisms of guidance cues

Molecular mechanisms of guidance cues. (a) Netrin 1 signaling. Netrin 1 bound DCC homodimers activate Rac and Cdc42. The activated Rac promotes Arp2/3‐mediated lamellipodial protrusion. Conversely, Netrin 1‐bound UNC5 activates RhoA, leading to axon repulsion. (b) Slit signaling. Slit binds to Robo and inactivates Cdc42 or stimulates Rac activity, which leads to actin depolymerization and repulsion. (c) Semaphorin signaling. The C‐terminal PDZ‐binding motif of Plexin interacts with Rho GEF, and semaphorin activation induces RhoA‐mediated repulsion. Activated RhoA promotes MLC phosphorylation via ROCK and triggers actomyosin bundle formation. RhoA via ROCK also activates LIMK and inhibits actin depolymerization. Plexin‐B1 also inhibits Rac by competing with PAK, which results in a repulsive effect. (d) Shh signaling. Shh binds to Boc and Ptch1, activating Smo and Src family kinases (SFKs). SFKs phosphorylate ZBP1, which then translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to corepressors and coactivators to regulate the transcription of specific target genes, ultimately enabling polarized actin polymerization. (e) BMP signaling. BMP induces attraction by regulating actin dynamics via ADF/Cofilin through LIMK and SSH phosphatase. Phosphorylated Smad recruits Smad4 and translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to corepressors and coactivators to regulate the transcription of specific target genes. (f) Wnt signaling. In the Wnt/Ca2⁺ pathway, calcium influx activates CaMKII, leading to a repulsive effect on the growth cone by regulating the reorganization of dynamic microtubules. The Wnt/PCP pathway, mediated by Frizzled and Dvl2, utilizes Rho family GTPases to regulate cytoskeletal rearrangements. In the Wnt/β‐catenin pathway, Wnt signaling inhibits GSK3β‐mediated β‐catenin degradation, allowing its nuclear accumulation and activation of target gene transcription. (g) CSPG signaling. Receptors for CSPGs are PTPσ, Nogo receptors, and Contactin 1. When CSPGs bind to PTPσ, they promote the dephosphorylation of its substrates, such as Cortactin. This leads to the inhibition of actin polymerization. (h) Nogo/MAG signaling. Nogo and MAG inhibit axonal outgrowth by activating the NgR signaling pathway. NgR functions together with co‐receptors, LINGO1/p75NTR/TROY, and activates RhoA, which leads to growth cone collapse. LOTUS binds to NgR1 and antagonizes Nogo‐NgR signaling. (i) Ephrin signaling. Eph forward signaling involves Ephexin, which connects Eph receptors to Rho GTPases, inducing growth cone collapse via RhoA‐ROCK. Reverse signaling by Ephrin‐B occurs when SH2 domain‐containing proteins, such as Grb4, bind to its phosphorylated tyrosine residues, activating FAK and promoting attraction. ADF, actin depolymerizing factor; Arp2/3, actin‐related protein 2/3 complex; BMP, bone morphogenetic protein; CaMKII, calcium/calmodulin‐dependent protein kinase II; Cdc42, cell division control protein 42 homolog; CSPGs, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans; Dvl2, Dishevelled segment polarity protein 2; FAK, focal adhesion kinase; LINGO 1, Leucine‐rich repeat and Ig domain containing 1; MTs, microtubules; NgR, Nogo receptor; Nogo, neurite outgrowth inhibitor; N‐WASP, Neural Wiskott‐Aldrich syndrome protein; PCP, planar cell polarity; p75NTR, p75 neurotrophin receptor; PTPσ, protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma; Rac, Ras‐related C3 botulinum toxin substrate; SFKs, Src family kinases; Smad, mothers against decapentaplegic homolog; TROY, Tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily, member 19; SSH, slingshot; UNC5, uncoordinated 5; ZBP1, zip code‐binding protein 1
